Short Description: Equity generated by federal and state tax credits for affordable rental housing.
Best Project Types: New construction, acquisition-rehab, preservation, PSH with strong subsidy.
Best Housing Models: LIHTC family, special needs, mixed-population PSH, ELI set-asides.
Best Populations Served: Low-income renters; TAY only when paired with referrals, services, and subsidy.
Typical Affordability Levels: Usually 30%-60% AMI; deeper units need rent subsidy.
Typical Award Size: Varies by eligible basis; often the largest equity source.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: 30%-70% of total development cost depending on 4% vs 9% structure.
Typical Term: 15-year federal compliance; commonly 55-year affordability in California.
Repayable: No, but equity has investor compliance obligations.
Application Timeline: Active 2026 cycles; 9% Round 2 due 2026-07-21; 4% Round 3 due 2026-09-08.
Sponsor Eligibility: Project owner or partnership meeting CTCAC/CDLAC rules.
Key Partners: Syndicator, investor, lender, CTCAC, CDLAC, public gap funders.
Major Advantages: Largest scalable capital source; bankable once awarded.
Major Limitations: Does not solve ELI rents, services, or youth referral pipeline.
Common Pairings: PBV, MHP, LACDA NOFA, AHTF, NPLH, HOME, CoC, DMH.
Why This Fits: Best chassis for permanent TAY housing when subsidies cover deep affordability.
Watch Out For: Youth mission must be supported by separate operating and service sources.

Administering Agency: HUD; local participating jurisdictions such as LACDA
Short Description: Federal gap funding for affordable housing, administered locally.
Best Project Types: Gap financing for multifamily new construction or rehab.
Best Housing Models: LIHTC rental housing, PSH, deeply affordable units with clear compliance plan.
Best Populations Served: Low-income households; TAY when units meet HOME and project targeting rules.
Typical Affordability Levels: HOME income/rent limits; often 30%-60% AMI depending on unit mix.
Typical Award Size: Varies; LACDA annual HOME allocation around $7.4M total.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Usually small-to-medium gap source, often under 15%.
Typical Term: Long affordability period; local loan term often aligned with other soft debt.
Repayable: Usually repayable soft loan or deferred loan locally.
Competitive or Formula: Formula to jurisdiction; competitive to projects.
Application Timeline: Active annual allocation; in LA County generally via LACDA NOFA when available.
Sponsor Eligibility: Local NOFA applicants meeting HOME and underwriting rules.
Key Partners: LACDA, city/county PJ, HUD environmental review, senior lenders.
Major Advantages: Flexible gap source that can fill difficult holes.
Major Limitations: High compliance burden; subsidy layering and environmental timing matter.
Common Pairings: LIHTC, AHTF, PBV, MHP, NPLH, private debt.
Development Stage: Gap financing after site and concept are defined.
Why This Fits: Can close a capital gap for TAY units in an otherwise financeable deal.
Watch Out For: Small HOME awards can create outsized compliance costs.

Administering Agency: California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD)
Short Description: State deferred-payment financing for affordable multifamily rental housing.
Best Project Types: Supportive housing, deeply affordable rental, 4% LIHTC gap projects.
Best Housing Models: PSH, special needs, ELI units, senior/family affordable housing with deep gaps.
Best Populations Served: Low-income and special-needs households; strong fit for homeless TAY units.
Typical Affordability Levels: Often 30%-60% AMI; special-needs units may be deeper.
Typical Award Size: Several million to tens of millions; subject to NOFA caps.
Typical Term: 55 years commonly used for state affordability.
Repayable: Yes, usually deferred-payment residual receipts loan.
Application Timeline: Current 2026 MHP Gap materials posted; window status can close quickly; monitor HCD.
Sponsor Eligibility: Qualified developers and owners meeting HCD guidelines.
Key Partners: HCD, tax credit investor, CDLAC/CTCAC, local gap lenders.
Major Advantages: Large state gap source; can support special-needs operating reserves.
Major Limitations: Competitive, complex, and timing-sensitive with bond/credit cycles.
Common Pairings: 4% LIHTC, PBV, LACDA NOFA, NPLH, HOME, private debt.
Development Stage: Advanced predevelopment through construction finance closing.
Why This Fits: Strong gap source for PSH or deeply affordable youth-serving buildings.
Watch Out For: Must align HCD timing with tax-exempt bond and 4% credit schedule.

Administering Agency: California HCD with public entity applicants
Short Description: Rapid production funding for PSH and conversions; current pathway is Homekey+.
Best Project Types: Adaptive reuse, acquisition-rehab, motel/hotel conversion, PSH new construction.
Best Housing Models: Permanent supportive housing with public sponsor and services plan.
Best Populations Served: People homeless or at risk with behavioral health challenges; may include TAY.
Typical Affordability Levels: Deeply affordable PSH; 55-year affordability for Homekey+ PSH.
Typical Award Size: Varies widely; can fund capital and capitalized operating subsidy.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Can be dominant source for acquisition/conversion; lower for gap-only uses.
Repayable: Often grant or forgivable structure; check NOFA and standard agreement.
Application Timeline: Homekey+ application window open and ongoing until funds are expended.
Sponsor Eligibility: Public entities and tribes; may apply jointly with nonprofit or for-profit co-applicants.
Site Control Required: Yes or clear path to control
Key Partners: City, county, housing authority, HCD, service provider, operator.
Major Advantages: Fast, large, and can include operating subsidy for PSH.
Major Limitations: Public agency partner is usually essential; target population is narrower under Homekey+.
Common Pairings: BHSA, DMH, PBV, local services, philanthropy, county operating funds.
Why This Fits: Strong for TAY PSH if youth also meet behavioral health and homelessness criteria.
Watch Out For: Do not treat legacy Homekey as a normal annual soft-loan program.

Program Name: Los Angeles County Development Authority Multifamily NOFA
Short Description: County competition for capital funds and PBVs in LACDA jurisdiction.
Best Project Types: New construction and acquisition-rehab outside City of Los Angeles.
Best Housing Models: General affordable, special needs, PSH, TAY set-aside within larger project.
Best Populations Served: Low-income, special-needs, homeless, and extremely low-income households.
Typical Affordability Levels: Includes required 30% AMI set-asides; broader mix often 30%-80% AMI.
Typical Award Size: Round 32 offered up to $90M total and up to $10M AHTF per project.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Major local gap source; often 10%-30% plus PBV value.
Typical Term: Long-term soft loan and affordability covenant.
Repayable: Yes, typically soft debt / residual receipts.
Application Timeline: Round 32 released 2026-04-23; applications due 2026-06-08; review active into July.
Sponsor Eligibility: Experienced affordable housing owners/developers meeting threshold requirements.
Key Partners: LACDA, service provider, PHA Section 8 team, tax credit team, local jurisdiction.
Major Advantages: Local capital plus PBV path in one application.
Major Limitations: Not for City of Los Angeles sites; competitive and readiness-heavy.
Common Pairings: LIHTC, AHTF, PBV, HOME, NPLH, MHP, DMH.
Why This Fits: Primary county-side doorway for local capital and project-based subsidy.
Watch Out For: Wrong front door for sites inside the City of Los Angeles.

Program Name: Los Angeles County Housing Innovation Fund
Short Description: Revolving acquisition and predevelopment loan fund for affordable housing.
Best Project Types: Site acquisition, predevelopment, bridge financing before public awards.
Best Housing Models: Affordable rental, PSH, acquisition-rehab, adaptive reuse pipeline projects.
Best Populations Served: Low-income and special-needs households depending on final project financing.
Typical Affordability Levels: Depends on final permanent sources; often 30%-80% AMI.
Typical Award Size: Fund size about $70M; loan size varies by lender and deal.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Early-stage bridge source, not permanent stack.
Application Timeline: Active revolving fund; intake depends on lending partners and fund capacity.
Sponsor Eligibility: Qualified affordable housing sponsors with viable takeout plan.
Key Partners: LACDA, Genesis LA, CDFIs, senior lender, public takeout funder.
Major Advantages: Moves faster than annual NOFA cycles for site control.
Major Limitations: Requires credible permanent financing takeout; not a subsidy source.
Common Pairings: LACDA NOFA, LIHTC, AHTF, MHP, PBV, philanthropy.
Why This Fits: Useful to secure TAY-appropriate sites before public funding cycles.
Watch Out For: Bridge debt can create pressure if NOFA or tax credit timing slips.

Program Name: Los Angeles County Affordable Housing Trust Fund
Short Description: County soft-capital source commonly deployed through LACDA NOFA.
Best Project Types: County affordable housing new construction and acquisition-rehab.
Best Housing Models: General affordable, PSH, mixed-population, special needs.
Best Populations Served: Low-income households; special-needs and homeless populations when prioritized.
Typical Affordability Levels: Often includes 30% AMI units; broader project mix can extend higher.
Typical Award Size: Round 32 AHTF cap listed at $10M per project.
Typical Term: Long-term affordability covenant and soft loan term.
Application Timeline: Active via LACDA NOFA cycles; Round 32 applications due 2026-06-08.
Sponsor Eligibility: Affordable housing developers meeting LACDA NOFA rules.
Key Partners: LACDA, County CEO, tax credit team, public lenders, service provider.
Major Advantages: Core LA County soft debt; highly relevant to local deals.
Major Limitations: Geography and NOFA timing control access.
Common Pairings: LIHTC, PBV, HOME, MHP, NPLH, private debt.
Development Stage: Advanced predevelopment and full financing application.
Why This Fits: Can serve as local gap capital for youth-serving affordable housing.
Watch Out For: Usually accessed through NOFA, not as a free-standing application.

Administering Agency: California HCD; Los Angeles County through LACDA and LACDMH
Short Description: Capital financing for PSH serving people with serious mental illness and homelessness risk.
Best Project Types: Permanent supportive housing with behavioral health targeting.
Best Housing Models: PSH, integrated special-needs units, service-rich LIHTC buildings.
Best Populations Served: Homeless or at-risk people needing mental health services; eligible TAY subset.
Typical Affordability Levels: Deeply affordable PSH, commonly 30% AMI or below with subsidy.
Typical Award Size: Varies by county allocation and project; often large soft-debt gap source.
Competitive or Formula: County allocation and competitive project selection.
Application Timeline: Active program; local availability through county/HCD NOFA cycles.
Sponsor Eligibility: Qualified PSH sponsors with county mental health partnership.
Key Partners: LACDMH, LACDA, HCD, service provider, PBV administrator.
Major Advantages: Very strong fit for clinically targeted TAY PSH.
Major Limitations: Not a general homeless youth source; behavioral health eligibility is central.
Common Pairings: LIHTC, PBV, LACDA NOFA, DMH contracts, MHP, philanthropy.
Development Stage: Advanced PSH concept through permanent financing.
Why This Fits: Best for TAY projects intentionally serving youth with serious behavioral health needs.
Watch Out For: Clinical referral and service infrastructure must be real, not appended later.

Administering Agency: HUD through local Public Housing Agencies
Short Description: Tenant-based Section 8 rent assistance that follows the household.
Best Project Types: Scattered-site leasing, lease-up support, move-up strategies.
Best Housing Models: Tenant-based rental housing, landlord partnership, scattered-site TAY units.
Best Populations Served: Low-income households with vouchers; TAY when eligible through PHA pathways.
Typical Affordability Levels: Tenant generally pays income-based rent; subsidy covers approved gap.
Typical Award Size: Per-household monthly subsidy; not a project award.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Not capital; weak for permanent debt sizing.
Typical Term: Annual PHA funding; assistance continues while tenant remains eligible.
Competitive or Formula: Formula to PHA; waitlist/referral to households.
Application Timeline: Active ongoing PHA program; waitlists and preferences vary by PHA.
Sponsor Eligibility: Household receives voucher; owner participates as landlord.
Key Partners: LACDA, HACLA, other PHAs, landlord, service provider.
Major Advantages: Portable and valuable for individual youth stability.
Major Limitations: Not dependable project revenue unless project-based.
Common Pairings: FYI, FUP, LAHSA navigation, philanthropy, landlord incentives.
Why This Fits: Good for scattered-site TAY housing and youth transitions from programs.
Watch Out For: Do not underwrite a new building assuming tenant-based vouchers will appear.

Administering Agency: HUD through local Public Housing Agencies
Short Description: Voucher subsidy attached to specific units under a HAP contract.
Best Project Types: New construction, rehab, PSH, deeply affordable LIHTC units.
Best Housing Models: Project-based supportive housing, ELI units, mixed-income LIHTC with set-asides.
Best Populations Served: ELI households; homeless and special-needs TAY when preferences/referrals align.
Typical Affordability Levels: Often 30% AMI or income-based tenant payment.
Typical Award Size: Monthly rental assistance per contracted unit; project value depends on rents and term.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Not capital, but can materially size permanent debt.
Typical Term: Initial HAP contract term often long-term subject to PHA rules.
Competitive or Formula: Competitive PHA selection unless noncompetitive pathway applies.
Application Timeline: Active via PHA processes; LACDA Round 32 included up to 300 PBVs with capital requests.
Sponsor Eligibility: Owner/developer selected by PHA and meeting PBV requirements.
Key Partners: PHA, LACDA or HACLA, property owner, service provider, lender, investor.
Major Advantages: Most underwritable rental subsidy for deeply affordable TAY units.
Major Limitations: PHA cap, procurement, inspections, subsidy layering, and jurisdiction limits.
Common Pairings: LIHTC, LACDA NOFA, AHTF, NPLH, HOME, MHP, DMH.
Why This Fits: Turns extremely low-income youth units into financeable project revenue.
Watch Out For: Tenant-based vouchers are not the same as PBVs for underwriting.

Administering Agency: HUD through PHAs with public child welfare agencies
Short Description: Special-purpose HCV assistance for eligible former foster youth ages 18-24.
Best Project Types: Scattered-site leasing, bridge to independent housing, youth lease-up pipeline.
Best Housing Models: Tenant-based TAY apartments, scattered-site supportive housing, move-on housing.
Best Populations Served: Former foster youth who are homeless or at risk of homelessness.
Typical Affordability Levels: Income-based tenant payment with voucher subsidy.
Typical Award Size: Per-youth monthly subsidy; not a capital award.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Not capital; limited underwriting value unless project-based.
Typical Term: 36 months, with possible 24-month extension if eligible.
Competitive or Formula: Noncompetitive rolling PHA requests; competitive NOFOs when issued.
Application Timeline: Active noncompetitive PHA request process; individual requests not accepted by HUD.
Sponsor Eligibility: PHA applies; child welfare agency must partner and secure supportive services.
Nonprofit Eligible: Yes, as service partner or landlord
Key Partners: PHA, DCFS, youth service provider, landlord, coordinated entry.
Major Advantages: Directly matches former foster youth target population.
Major Limitations: Time-limited and tenant-based; not a building finance source.
Common Pairings: HCV, FUP, LAHSA services, philanthropy, landlord incentives.
Why This Fits: One of the most targeted subsidy tools for former foster youth.
Watch Out For: Developers need a PHA and child welfare pathway, not a direct application.

Administering Agency: HUD through PHAs with public child welfare agencies
Short Description: Special-purpose HCV for child-welfare families and eligible foster youth.
Best Project Types: Scattered-site leasing, child welfare housing stabilization, move-on housing.
Best Housing Models: Tenant-based apartments, family reunification units, youth transition housing.
Typical Affordability Levels: Income-based tenant payment with voucher subsidy.
Typical Award Size: Per-household monthly subsidy; not a capital award.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Not capital; limited underwriting value unless project-based.
Typical Term: Youth assistance is time-limited; family assistance can be ongoing.
Competitive or Formula: HUD awards to PHAs; tenant referrals via child welfare partners.
Application Timeline: Active where PHA has FUP allocation; new HUD competitions vary.
Sponsor Eligibility: PHA applies; PCWA referral partnership required.
Key Partners: PHA, DCFS, service provider, landlord, child welfare courts as relevant.
Major Advantages: Strong child-welfare fit and can support both youth and families.
Major Limitations: Tenant-based and PHA-controlled; project underwriting value is weak.
Common Pairings: FYI, HCV, LAHSA services, philanthropy, supportive services.
Why This Fits: Relevant for TAY coming from foster care and for reunification stability.
Watch Out For: Project-basing requires a separate PHA decision and process.

Program Name: Continuum of Care Permanent Supportive Housing Rental Assistance
Administering Agency: HUD; Los Angeles CoC via LAHSA as Collaborative Applicant
Short Description: CoC funding for PSH rental assistance, leasing, services, and operations.
Best Project Types: PSH renewals, project-based or sponsor-based rental assistance, youth PSH.
Best Housing Models: Permanent supportive housing, sponsor-based rental assistance, project-based RA.
Best Populations Served: Homeless people with disabilities; TAY if eligible and prioritized locally.
Typical Affordability Levels: Income-based tenant contribution; deeply affordable PSH.
Typical Award Size: Annual grant amount varies by project and unit count.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Not capital; can support NOI if long-term rental assistance is committed.
Typical Term: Annual grants with renewal process; rental assistance can be long-term.
Competitive or Formula: Annual competitive CoC process and renewals.
Application Timeline: Active annual CoC process; LAHSA posts local policies and ranking materials.
Sponsor Eligibility: Nonprofits, states, local governments, and instrumentalities; not for-profit grantees.
Site Control Required: Depends; yes for project-based real estate applications.
Key Partners: LAHSA, CoC board, service provider, owner, HMIS, coordinated entry.
Major Advantages: Can provide long-term PSH rental assistance and services.
Major Limitations: Annual competition, match, renewal risk, and local system dependence.
Common Pairings: LIHTC, PBV, NPLH, DMH, LAHSA services, philanthropy.
Development Stage: Program design through operations; best when award is committed.
Why This Fits: Strong for homeless TAY PSH when eligibility and CoC ranking align.
Watch Out For: Speculative future CoC awards are hard to underwrite at construction closing.

Administering Agency: HUD; Los Angeles CoC via LAHSA
Short Description: Youth homelessness demonstration funding for coordinated community approaches.
Best Project Types: Youth PSH, rapid rehousing, coordinated entry, navigation, system pilots.
Best Housing Models: Youth-specific PSH, RRH, host homes, navigation, CES enhancements.
Best Populations Served: Youth and young adults experiencing homelessness.
Typical Affordability Levels: Varies by funded model; rental assistance usually income-based.
Typical Award Size: Project-specific grants; Los Angeles received a major community award.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Usually operating/rental/program support, not capital stack.
Typical Term: Grant terms and renewals vary by project.
Competitive or Formula: Competitive community selection and local project selection.
Application Timeline: Active in Los Angeles through LAHSA youth scopes; no generic developer window.
For-Profit Eligible: Generally no as HUD CoC grantee/subrecipient
Key Partners: LAHSA, Youth Action Board, service providers, CoC, landlords, PHAs.
Major Advantages: Highly aligned with youth homelessness and flexible model design.
Major Limitations: Demonstration/system money; not a conventional project finance source.
Common Pairings: CoC, LAHSA services, FYI, FUP, philanthropy, PBV.
Development Stage: Program design, referrals, operations, youth system integration.
Why This Fits: Directly supports youth homelessness system capacity around TAY housing.
Watch Out For: Do not rely on it as construction or permanent debt support.

Administering Agency: DHCS framework; county behavioral health departments implement
Short Description: Prop 1/BHSA framework allowing behavioral health housing supports.
Best Project Types: PSH operations, rental subsidy, service-linked housing, behavioral health housing supports.
Best Housing Models: PSH, shared housing, family housing, operating subsidy, housing navigation.
Best Populations Served: People with significant behavioral health needs; eligible TAY subset.
Typical Affordability Levels: Deep affordability when used for subsidy or operating support.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Usually operating/services, not capital; can stabilize underwriting indirectly.
Application Timeline: Active implementation; access through county planning and contracts, not direct developer window.
Sponsor Eligibility: County-contracted providers and partners serving eligible populations.
Key Partners: LACDMH, DHCS, service providers, housing operators, managed care plans.
Major Advantages: Potentially foundational for operating and service gaps.
Major Limitations: Still implementation-dependent; not a simple application program.
Common Pairings: Homekey+, NPLH, DMH contracts, PBV, LIHTC, philanthropy.
Why This Fits: Relevant for TAY projects with behavioral health needs and service intensity.
Watch Out For: Must match county BHSA priorities and eligible populations.

Program Name: Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health Contracts
Administering Agency: Los Angeles County Department of Mental Health (LACDMH)
Short Description: County mental health contracts and housing programs supporting PSH and services.
Best Project Types: Clinically targeted PSH, TAY service partnerships, operating subsidy-linked housing.
Best Housing Models: PSH, full-service partnership housing, TAY project-based operating subsidy.
Best Populations Served: TAY with serious mental illness, serious emotional disturbance, or intensive service needs.
Typical Affordability Levels: Deeply affordable PSH; rent often supported by subsidy.
Typical Award Size: Contract-specific; service and operating subsidy amounts vary.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Operating/services, not capital; can improve feasibility.
Typical Term: County contract terms and renewals vary.
Repayable: No, generally contract reimbursement or subsidy.
Application Timeline: Active programs; access through LACDMH contracts and housing divisions.
Sponsor Eligibility: Qualified providers, operators, and housing partners under county rules.
Key Partners: LACDMH, service provider, LACDA/HACLA, owner, managed care partners.
Major Advantages: Critical for service-rich TAY PSH and clinical referral pathways.
Major Limitations: Best fit only when behavioral health targeting is authentic.
Common Pairings: NPLH, Homekey+, PBV, CoC, LIHTC, philanthropy.
Why This Fits: Can supply the operating and clinical backbone for TAY PSH.
Watch Out For: A housing developer likely needs a credible mental health provider partner.

Program Name: Los Angeles Homeless Services Authority Service Contracts
Short Description: Local homelessness system contracts for services, interim housing, navigation, and subsidies.
Best Project Types: TAY interim housing, host homes, navigation, time-limited subsidies, CES services.
Best Housing Models: Youth homelessness services, RRH, TLS, interim housing, housing navigation.
Best Populations Served: People experiencing homelessness, including TAY and unaccompanied minors.
Typical Affordability Levels: Varies by service model; often supports deep affordability indirectly.
Typical Award Size: Contract-specific; varies by scope and service volume.
Typical Term: Annual or multi-year contract cycles depending on funding source.
Application Timeline: FY25-26 resources active; FY26-27 updates underway; procurement varies.
Sponsor Eligibility: Homeless service providers and contracted agencies meeting LAHSA requirements.
Key Partners: LAHSA, CES, service providers, landlords, DCFS, DMH, PHAs.
Major Advantages: Central to local TAY homelessness service system.
Major Limitations: Reimbursement and renewal risk; not stable enough alone for debt underwriting.
Common Pairings: YHDP, CoC, FYI, FUP, HHAP, philanthropy, PBV.
Why This Fits: Connects the project to the youth homelessness delivery system.
Watch Out For: Diversify funding; contracts may not be bankable permanent revenue.

Program Name: Homeless Housing, Assistance and Prevention Program
Administering Agency: California HCD; local governments and CoCs allocate funds
Short Description: Flexible state homelessness funding allocated to local jurisdictions and CoCs.
Best Project Types: Youth set-asides, launch costs, landlord incentives, shallow subsidies, navigation.
Best Housing Models: RRH, prevention, interim housing, operating support, youth services.
Best Populations Served: People experiencing or at risk of homelessness; youth set-aside required in current round.
Typical Affordability Levels: Varies; can support extremely low-income households through subsidies.
Typical Award Size: Large local allocations; project/subcontract amounts vary.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Usually operating/program support, not capital stack.
Typical Term: Round-specific expenditure deadlines and local contracts.
Competitive or Formula: Formula allocation to eligible jurisdictions; local subawards may be competitive.
Application Timeline: HHAP Round 6 state application window closed; local awarded allocations remain active.
Sponsor Eligibility: Direct grantees are jurisdictions/CoCs; providers access through local contracts.
Site Control Required: No for system funding; depends on local project.
Key Partners: HCD, LA County, City of LA, LAHSA, service providers, landlords.
Major Advantages: Flexible homelessness dollars with required youth focus.
Major Limitations: Not usually long-term mortgageable revenue; local plan controls use.
Common Pairings: LAHSA contracts, YHDP, CoC, philanthropy, FYI, FUP.
Development Stage: Program design, launch, operations, system capacity.
Why This Fits: Flexible support can pay for the pieces vouchers and capital do not cover.
Watch Out For: Need local allocation strategy and contract pathway, not just state eligibility.

Administering Agency: Foundations, donor collaboratives, and philanthropic funds
Short Description: Flexible grants or guarantees for model launch, services, evaluation, and risk coverage.
Best Project Types: Pilots, launch-year staffing, reserves, landlord mitigation, evaluation, capacity.
Best Housing Models: TAY demonstration projects, scattered-site, sponsor-based, supportive services models.
Best Populations Served: TAY, former foster youth, youth experiencing homelessness, special populations.
Typical Affordability Levels: Can support deepest affordability indirectly but rarely sets rent restrictions alone.
Typical Share of Capital Stack: Small but catalytic; usually under 10% unless PRI/guarantee structure.
Typical Term: 1-3 years common; PRIs/guarantees may be longer.
Repayable: Usually no for grants; yes for PRI or recoverable grant.
Application Timeline: Active but variable; funder-specific windows and invitations.
Sponsor Eligibility: Usually nonprofits; fiscally sponsored projects often eligible; for-profits need structure.
For-Profit Eligible: Sometimes, usually through PRI or partnership
Key Partners: Hilton Foundation, California Community Foundation, local family foundations, CDFIs.
Major Advantages: Most flexible source for gaps public programs do not cover.
Major Limitations: Not durable underwriting revenue and often not renewable.
Common Pairings: All public programs, especially FYI, FUP, LAHSA, CoC, PBV, DMH.
Why This Fits: Can backstop vacancies, services, youth engagement, and early proof of concept.
Watch Out For: Should not replace durable rental subsidy or county service contracts.
